Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in caring for new mothers’ emotional health. Over the next few minutes we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. This is simply a screening tool; it’s not a pass-or-fail test, and every answer stays confidential within our care team. We’ll go through ten short questions about the past seven days; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—pretty much every day, actually. My husband made a goofy face while changing the baby’s diaper yesterday and I burst out laughing, so… I guess I’m finding the humor in things.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’d say most of the time—like, every day I’ve found something to laugh at. Maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but definitely still happening.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yeah, I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee or when my sister visits with lunch. They’re smaller things than before, but I do get that little spark of “oh, that’ll be nice.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up right after I’ve changed her outfit, I might think, “Well, maybe I shouldn’t have laid her down so fast,” but I don’t sit there beating myself up. It’s more like, “Okay, next time I’ll wait a minute.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, maybe. Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing sounds different, even when she’s perfectly fine. It’s quick—like a flash—and then I check her and I’m okay again. Doesn’t happen all day, but it pops up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that kind of sudden panic. I get those little “what-if” worries about the baby, but it never turns into actual fear or a racing heart.
Things have been getting on top of me

I mean, yeah, some days feel like a juggling act—feed the baby, wash the bottles, try to shower, answer texts—but it’s not overwhelming. I just take it one task at a time and eventually it all gets done.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve actually been sleeping pretty well—well, as well as anyone whose nights are broken up every few hours by a hungry baby. Once I’m back in bed I drift right off.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt really sad or miserable. Tired, sure, and maybe a little wistful for the easy days before diapers, but nothing close to miserable.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not at all. I think I’ve teared up once when the baby wouldn’t latch and my nipples were sore, but it was more frustration than unhappiness, and it passed in a minute.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I want to stick around and watch her grow.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (self-report via EPDS-style questions)  

**Main symptoms/concerns**  
- Mild, situational “what-if” worries about infant well-being (Q4) – no pervasive panic or generalized anxiety  
- Occasional “juggling” stress; denies feeling overwhelmed or persistently low (Q6)  
- No anhedonia: continues to anticipate and enjoy small daily activities (Q2)  
- No excessive guilt, self-blame, crying spells, sleep-mood linkage, or thoughts of self-harm (Q3, Q7–Q10)  

**Pattern summary**  
Endorses brief, infant-focused worries that resolve quickly with reassurance. Affect remains generally positive; coping strategies intact. No indicators of major depressive or anxiety episode.  

**Screening significance / risk factors**  
- Current findings do not meet threshold for probable postpartum depression or anxiety disorder  
- Continue routine psychoeducation and monitor for escalation of worries or mood changes at follow-up  
- Safety: nil concerns expressed or elicited
